title: Serverless Execution Architecture: How Platforms Start Functions Without Persistent Processes
description:
Serverless Execution Architecture: How Platforms Start Functions Without Persistent Processes

Serverless platforms decouple application code from persistent infrastructure by dynamically orchestrating execution environments on demand. Rather than keeping every registered function running continuously, modern function-as-a-service (FaaS) systems leverage intelligent schedulers, isolated execution runtimes, and lifecycle management controllers to provision compute resources only when invocation events occur.

Understanding how serverless architectures orchestrate this on-demand lifecycle requires analyzing the end-to-end request path, the mechanics of cold versus warm execution, and the underlying multi-tenant isolation boundaries.

[Invocation Request]
        │
        ▼
[API Gateway / Router]
        │
        ▼
[Function Scheduler / Dispatcher]
        ├──> [Warm Execution Environment] ──(Reuse)──> [Handler Execution]
        └──> [Cold Provisioning] 
                  ├──> Allocate VM / Sandbox
                  ├──> Pull Code & Dependencies
                  ├──> Initialize Runtime & Global State
                  └──> Execute Handler

1. Architectural Taxonomy & Core Trade-offs

When designing distributed systems, engineers must weigh the operational overhead of persistent infrastructure against the runtime unpredictability of serverless execution. FaaS platforms eliminate idle capacity costs by scaling down to zero, but they trade away deterministic latency profiles and continuous memory residency.

The Lifecycle of a Serverless Invocation

Every serverless execution traverses a well-defined state machine governed by the platform control plane and data plane routers:

  1. Invocation Request: An external trigger (HTTP webhook, storage event, message queue payload) hits the platform's ingress tier.
  2. Function Scheduler: The scheduler inspects the target function's namespace, current concurrency metrics, and region availability to locate an existing warm environment or request a new one.
  3. Execution Environment Allocation: If a warm container or micro-VM is available, the request is routed immediately. If no environment exists, the scheduler signals the provisioning layer.
  4. Runtime Initialization: The platform allocates a lightweight sandbox (using technologies such as lightweight hypervisors or container namespaces), mounts the deployment package, and boots the runtime interpreter.
  5. Handler Execution: The runtime executes the entrypoint function, passing the event payload and context object.
  6. Response Lifecycle: The handler returns a response or error, which streams back through the API gateway while the execution environment transitions into an idle state, awaiting subsequent invocations.

2. Multi-Variable Comparison Matrix

Evaluating compute models requires balancing cold-start penalties, scaling agility, and infrastructure management overhead against steady-state execution costs.

Architectural Metric Serverless (FaaS) Container Orchestration (Kubernetes) Dedicated Virtual Machines
Startup Latency Variable (Milliseconds to Seconds for Cold Starts) Low to Moderate (Seconds for Container Pulls) High (Minutes for OS Boot and Provisioning)
Scaling Granularity Per-request or per-event concurrency Per-pod or node-level autoscaling Manual or instance-group scaling
Idle Resource Cost Zero (scales to zero instances) Non-zero (minimum node pool reservation) Fixed cost per provisioned instance
Maximum Execution Duration Bounded (typically 15-minute hard limit) Unbounded Unbounded
Operational Overhead Low (code-centric packaging) High (cluster management, networking, patching) High (OS configuration, security hardening)

3. Architectural Deep Dive

Cold vs. Warm Execution Mechanics

The fundamental performance differentiator in serverless computing is whether an invocation hits a warm or cold environment.

[Cold Start Path]
Request ──> Scheduler ──> Sandbox Allocation (VM/Micro-VM) ──> Code Loading ──> Runtime Init ──> Handler (High Latency)

[Warm Start Path]
Request ──> Scheduler ──> Existing Idle Sandbox ───────────────────────────────────────────────> Handler (Low Latency)
  • Warm Execution: An existing execution environment retains its memory state, loaded dependencies, and active connection pools from a previous invocation. The scheduler routes incoming traffic directly to this environment, bypassing initialization overhead.
  • New Environment Creation: When concurrent requests exceed active warm instances, or when an environment has been reaped due to inactivity, the platform must initialize a fresh sandbox.
  • Runtime Startup & Dependency Loading: The platform mounts the deployment artifact, spins up the language runtime (Node.js, Python, Go, Rust), and executes global module-level code outside the handler function.
  • Initialization Impact: Any heavy computational logic, synchronous network calls, or large dependency graphs executed during module loading directly increase first-request latency. This directly mirrors how operating systems handle Virtual Memory Management How Operating Systems Handle Memory Limits when paging large binaries into active memory tables.

Why Cold Starts Happen

Cold starts are not random anomalies; they are deterministic outcomes of platform scaling mechanics:

  • New Traffic Bursts: Sudden spikes in incoming events outpace the platform's predictive scaling algorithms, requiring rapid parallel environment creation.
  • Scaling Events & Concurrency Limits: Exceeding an existing environment's concurrent request capacity forces the scheduler to provision additional parallel instances.
  • Environment Expiration: Platforms periodically recycle idle sandboxes to reclaim memory, clear cached state, and apply security patches.
  • Deployment Changes: Uploading new function code or modifying environment variables invalidates all existing warm environments across the fleet.
  • Infrastructure Placement: Scaling across availability zones or re-allocating workloads due to physical host degradation introduces allocation overhead.

What Determines Startup Latency?

The duration of a cold start is governed by several compounding variables:

  • Runtime Selection: Compiled runtimes with small static binaries (e.g., Go, Rust) initialize faster than interpreted or virtual-machine-based runtimes that require heavy JIT compilation or classpath scanning (e.g., Java, .NET).
  • Package Size: Uncompressed deployment archive size dictates how quickly storage layers stream code into the local execution sandbox.
  • Dependency Graph: Complex modular imports require disk I/O and symbol resolution before the application loop can accept traffic.
  • CPU Allocation: Most serverless platforms tie CPU allocation linearly or proportionally to memory configuration. Selecting a lower memory tier (e.g., 128 MB) often throttles CPU burst capacity during initialization, artificially inflating cold-start durations.

Scaling, Concurrency, and Database Connection Bottlenecks

Serverless scaling introduces unique challenges for downstream dependencies, particularly relational databases.

  • Concurrency Models: Some platforms process one request per execution environment, spawning hundreds of parallel containers during traffic surges. Others allow multi-threaded or asynchronous concurrent execution within a single environment.
  • Database Connection Storms: When 500 isolated function instances simultaneously cold-start and each open 5 database connections, the database instantly receives 2,500 new TCP connections. This easily overwhelms connection limits, triggering database failovers or catastrophic cascading timeouts.
  • Mitigation Patterns: Serverless architectures must implement connection pooling proxies (such as RDS Proxy), aggressive backpressure handling, and asynchronous queuing layers (analogous to patterns found in [Distributed Message Queues Preventing Slow Consumer Outages with Backpressure](https://wantsvibes.online/article/distributed-message-queues-preventing-slow-consumer-outages-with-backpressure/)) to protect upstream and downstream data layers.

4. Reconciled TCO Financial Model

To evaluate the economic viability of serverless platforms compared to dedicated container fleets, consider a production workload processing 30,000,000 requests per month, with an average execution duration of 200 milliseconds and an allocation of 512 MB RAM.

Financial Assumptions & Unit Conventions

  • Unit Convention: Decimal storage and compute metrics (1 GB = 1,000 MB).
  • Invocation Cost: $0.20 per 1,000,000 requests.
  • Compute Duration Cost: $0.0000166667 per GB-second.
  • Dedicated Container Baseline: Two redundant nodes (e.g., t4g.medium equivalents) running 24/7 to guarantee baseline capacity for burst handling.

Itemized Monthly Cost Calculation

1. Serverless Model (Pay-Per-Use):

  • Total Compute GB-seconds = 30,000,000 requests × (0.2 seconds/request) × (0.5 GB RAM) = 3,000,000 GB-seconds.
  • Compute Cost = 3,000,000 GB-seconds × $0.0000166667 = $50.00
  • Request Cost = 30,000,000 / 1,000,000 × $0.20 = $6.00
  • Total Serverless Monthly Cost: $56.00

2. Dedicated Container Model (Always-On Baseline):

  • Instance Rate: $30.00 per instance/month.
  • Baseline Infrastructure (2 instances) = 2 × $30.00 = $60.00
  • Load Balancer & Egress overhead = $15.00
  • Total Container Monthly Cost: $75.00

Note: Public cloud pricing rates are illustrative estimates subject to regional variations, sustained usage discounts, and enterprise tiering. At low-to-moderate or highly variable traffic volumes, serverless yields lower total cost. However, as execution volume approaches 100% sustained utilization, dedicated compute models become more economically predictable.

5. Illustrative Configuration

Below is an illustrative infrastructure configuration demonstrating serverless function provisioning alongside a database proxy to manage connection pooling during scaling events.

# Illustrative Terraform Configuration for Serverless Function & Connection Proxy

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "lambda_execution" {
  name = "production_lambda_execution_role"

  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [
      {
        Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
        Effect = "Allow"
        Principal = {
          Service = "lambda.amazonaws.com"
        }
      }
    ]
  })
}

resource "aws_lambda_function" "api_handler" {
  filename      = "lambda_payload.zip"
  function_name = "core_api_processor"
  role          = aws_iam_role.lambda_execution.arn
  handler       = "index.handler"
  runtime       = "nodejs20.x"
  memory_size   = 512
  timeout       = 15

  environment {
    variables = {
      DB_HOST = aws_db_proxy.database_proxy.endpoint
      NODE_ENV = "production"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_db_proxy" "database_proxy" {
  name                   = "serverless-db-proxy"
  engine_family          = "POSTGRESQL"
  auth {
    auth_scheme = "SECRETS"
    iam_auth    = "DISABLED"
    secret_arn  = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:db-credentials"
  }
  role_arn               = aws_iam_role.lambda_execution.arn
  vpc_subnet_ids         = ["subnet-0bb1c3a1", "subnet-0bb1c3a2"]
  require_tls            = true
}

6. Production Decision CTA Rubric

Architects must evaluate workload characteristics rigorously before committing to a serverless paradigm. Use the following rubric to determine architectural fit:

Serverless Is Highly Recommended When:

  • Workloads exhibit erratic, bursty traffic patterns with long periods of zero utilization.
  • Architecture relies heavily on asynchronous event-driven triggers (storage uploads, webhook ingestion, queue consumers).
  • Time-to-market and developer velocity outweigh granular infrastructure tuning.
  • Total compute consumption remains low enough that pay-per-invocation billing undercuts fixed baseline instance costs.

Alternatives Are Preferable When:

  • Workloads maintain consistent, high-utilization compute requirements 24/7.
  • Strict, deterministic sub-millisecond tail latency requirements preclude cold-start anomalies.
  • Applications require persistent TCP connection pools, in-memory state caching across requests, or long-running stream processing exceeding execution duration limits.
  • Specialized runtime configurations, custom kernel modules, or hardware accelerators (GPUs/TPUs) are mandatory.

title: Partial Failures Architecture: Designing Distributed Systems for Resiliency and Recovery
description:
Partial Failures Architecture: Designing Distributed Systems for Resiliency and Recovery

Modern distributed architectures operate under the constant reality that components fail independently, asynchronously, and silently. Unlike monolithic systems where a total hardware or process crash brings down the execution context uniformly, distributed systems experience partial failures. A node might lose network connectivity while its CPU is fully operational; a downstream dependency might suffer from garbage collection (GC) pauses while maintaining an open TCP socket; or packet loss across an availability zone boundary might degrade throughput without triggering an outright transport-layer RST packet.

Mastering this domain requires viewing systems through the lens of partial degradation. When building high-throughput pipelines—much like managing distributed cloud storage architecture how object systems survive server failures—engineers cannot rely on simplistic binary up/down states. This document establishes an architectural blueprint and Request for Comments (RFC) for designing detection, isolation, and recovery layers capable of handling partial failures without inducing cascading degradation.

1. Context & Problem Statement

Binary health models ("is the process responding?") fail in complex distributed topologies because partial failures manifest in nuanced ways. A system may process 95% of requests successfully while the remaining 5% hang indefinitely due to resource contention, connection pool exhaustion, or downstream lock contention.

[ Client Request ] 
       │
       ▼
 [ API Gateway ] ──(Connection Pool Exhaustion)──> [ Microservice A ]
       │                                                 │
       ├────── (Success: Fast Path) ─────────────────────┤
       │                                                 ▼
       └────── (Hang: Slow Dependency) ──────────> [ Downstream DB ]
                                                         │
                                                  (Thread Starvation)

Why Partial Failure Is Different

Process failure is straightforward: a process exits, an operating system reclaims resources, and a supervisor restarts or isolates the unit. Network failure, however, presents ambiguity. A severed cable, a saturated switch fabric, or an asymmetric routing table change can cause one-way packet loss, making it impossible for Node A to determine whether Node B is dead, slow, or merely unable to reply.

Slow responses are often more dangerous than outright crashes. When a dependency slows down, incoming requests accumulate in thread pools or event loops. This consumes memory, starves un-impacted code paths, and causes callers to time out and retry. This dynamic turns a localized performance bottleneck into a distributed failure amplifier.

2. Architectural Decision Record (ADR)

ADR-01: Adoption of Layered Failure Detection and Adaptive Circuit Breaking

Status

Accepted

Context

Our distributed topology spans multiple availability zones and relies on synchronous RPCs and asynchronous messaging. Standard liveness probes and fixed timeouts frequently generate false positives during temporary hypervisor CPU throttling or trigger retry storms during network jitter spikes.

Decision

We will decouple liveness from readiness, implement active failure detectors using phi accrual algorithms, enforce adaptive timeouts backed by historical latency percentiles, and mandate circuit breakers with randomized exponential backoff and jitter across all inter-service communication.

Consequences

  • Positive Trade-Offs: Eliminates false-positive node evictions during transient network blips; prevents thread starvation through aggressive shed policies; bounds blast radii when dependencies degrade.
  • Negative Trade-Offs: Increases architectural complexity; requires distributed coordination or local sliding-window telemetry collection; introduces minor overhead for latency tracking data structures.

Alternatives Considered

  • Fixed Threshold Timeouts: Rejected because static timeouts cannot adapt to fluctuating network topologies and varying payload sizes, leading to premature cancellation under normal load variations.
  • Binary Health Checks Only: Rejected because an HTTP 200 response on a /healthz endpoint does not verify whether database connection pools are exhausted or whether worker threads are deadlocked.

3. System Topology

The following ASCII diagram illustrates the separation of concerns across the detection, traffic-management, retry, and state-recovery layers:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT LAYER                        │
│  [ API Gateway / Load Balancer ] ──(Shedding / Rate Limit)──> [Proxy]  │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          DETECTION LAYER                               │
│  [ Phi Accrual Failure Detector ] ◄──(Heartbeat)──> [ Worker Node ]    │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     RETRY / CIRCUIT-BREAKER LAYER                      │
│  [ Circuit Breaker: Closed / Open / Half-Open ]                        │
│  [ Exponential Backoff + Full Jitter Engine ]                          │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        STATE-RECOVERY LAYER                            │
│  [ Write-Ahead Log ] ──> [ Checkpointing ] ──> [ Replay Engine ]       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4. Component Interface Signatures

To standardize partial failure handling across microservices, all inter-service communication modules must implement the following structural interfaces (represented here in abstract schema specifications):

syntax = "proto3";
package failsafe.v1;

enum CircuitState {
  CIRCUIT_STATE_UNSPECIFIED = 0;
  CIRCUIT_STATE_CLOSED = 1;
  CIRCUIT_STATE_OPEN = 2;
  CIRCUIT_STATE_HALF_OPEN = 3;
}

message HealthProbeRequest {
  string node_id = 1;
  int64 timestamp_ms = 2;
}

message HealthProbeResponse {
  string node_id = 1;
  CircuitState current_state = 2;
  double saturation_ratio = 3;
  int64 active_thread_count = 4;
}

message ExecutionContext {
  string correlation_id = 1;
  int32 retry_count = 2;
  int64 timeout_budget_ms = 3;
}

service FailsafeExecutor {
  rpc ExecuteWithProtection (HealthProbeRequest) returns (HealthProbeResponse);
}

5. Distributed Failure Domains and Detection Mechanics

Effective failure management begins with precise boundary identification and accurate detection mechanics. Redundancy provides no protection if failures are correlated across domains.

Failure Domains

Architectures must be analyzed across six distinct boundaries:

  1. Process: Individual runtime instances (e.g., container namespaces, JVM processes).
  2. Host: Physical or virtual machine instances sharing a hypervisor kernel or local disk controller.
  3. Rack: Top-of-rack (ToR) switches and power distribution units (PDUs).
  4. Availability Zone (AZ): Isolated datacenters with independent power, cooling, and network entry points.
  5. Region: Geographically distinct regions connected by wide-area network (WAN) links.
  6. Dependency: Shared external services (e.g., third-party identity providers, managed database clusters).

Active vs. Passive Detection

  • Active Detection: Probing nodes via periodic ping/pong messages or HTTP requests. While simple, active checks consume bandwidth and can saturate networks if probe intervals are too short.
  • Passive Detection: Inferring node health by monitoring actual client request traffic (e.g., tracking TCP retransmissions, HTTP 5xx responses, or connection timeouts). Passive detection scales efficiently with traffic volume but cannot detect failures on idle nodes.

The Timeout Problem and Mitigation

No universally correct timeout exists. Network latency varies across regions, queueing delays spike under load, and garbage collection pauses freeze runtimes unpredictably. Short timeouts trigger false positives and unnecessary failovers; long timeouts trap execution threads and starve callers.

Mitigate this by implementing adaptive timeouts tied to sliding-window latency percentiles ($p_{99}$), coupled with execution budgets that decrement across downstream RPC hops. Furthermore, implementing reliable data transfer mechanisms—similar to strategies used in distributed message queues preventing slow consumer outages with backpressure—ensures that downstream saturation does not cascade back upstream.

6. Health Checks vs. Real Health

A process responding successfully to /healthz does not guarantee that it can perform useful work. Health verification must be multi-tiered:

  • Liveness Probes: Verify that the event loop or main thread is unblocked and the process is running. A failure here warrants a container restart.
  • Readiness Probes: Verify that the service can accept traffic, checking local cache initialization, connection pool availability, and downstream storage responsiveness.
  • Dependency-Aware Health: Aggregate health signals from critical downstream dependencies. If a required database is unreachable, the service must report unreadiness to remove itself from load-balancer rotation before callers experience connection timeouts.

7. What Happens After Failure Detection

Once a failure is detected, the system must execute defensive control flows to limit the blast radius:

Traffic Removal and Replica Promotion

Load balancers must instantly unregister unhealthy instances based on readiness signals or active failure detector outputs. In stateful clusters, replica promotion protocols (e.g., Raft leader election) must elect a healthy follower with minimal replication lag.

Circuit Breaking and Request Shedding

Circuit breakers protect failing dependencies by short-circuiting calls when error rates cross configurable thresholds (e.g., >50% failure over a 10-second sliding window). When internal queues exceed capacity, request shedding drops low-priority traffic immediately with HTTP 429 or 503 responses rather than letting requests queue up and time out.

8. Retry Storms\, Jitter\, and Idempotency

Uncoordinated retries are primary contributors to cascading outages. When a service experiences transient latency, thousands of clients retrying simultaneously can multiply load by an order of magnitude.

Client Retry Wave 1: ──> [ Service (Normal Load: 100%) ]
Client Retry Wave 2: ──> [ Service (Overloaded: 400%) ] ──> [ Crash ]

Mitigation Strategies

  • Exponential Backoff: Increase delay between successive retry attempts exponentially ($t = \text{base} \times 2^{\text{attempt}}$).
  • Full Jitter: Add randomized jitter to the backoff interval to decorrelate retry spikes across independent clients: $$\ text{Sleep} = \text{Random}(0, \min(\text{MaxBackoff}, \text{Base} \times 2^{\text{attempt}}))$$
  • Retry Budgets: Restrict total retries across an application instance to a fixed percentage of total outgoing requests (e.g., maximum 10% retries) to prevent retry traffic from overwhelming recovering services.
  • Idempotency: Enforce idempotency keys across all write operations so that retried requests execute safely without duplicating side effects.

9. State Recovery and Cascading Failure Prevention

When recovering from partial failures, stateful services must reconcile data consistency without corrupting persistent stores.

Stateless vs. Stateful Recovery

  • Stateless Services: Recover instantly by spinning up new container instances behind a load balancer. State is externalized to databases or caches.
  • Stateful Services: Require write-ahead logs (WAL), periodic checkpointing, and deterministic log replay to rebuild in-memory state after a crash.

Preventing Cascading Failures

Cascading failures occur when resource exhaustion propagates upstream. Prevent this by pairing strict connection pooling limits with aggressive load shedding, bulkhead isolation (separating thread pools for different dependencies), and circuit breaking.

10. Observability and Failure Testing

Operational verification requires robust metrics to distinguish application failures from infrastructure anomalies.

Key Telemetry Signals

  • Error Rate: Ratio of HTTP 5xx responses and transport-layer exceptions to total traffic.
  • Latency Percentiles: Track $p_{50}$, $p_{95}$, $p_{99}$, and $p_{99.9}$ to spot tail latency anomalies before timeouts trigger.
  • Saturation: Measure CPU utilization, memory pressure, thread pool queue depths, and file descriptor limits.
  • Recovery Time: Track Time-To-Detect (TTD) and Time-To-Mitigate (TTM) across all failure scenarios.

Failure Testing (Chaos Engineering)

Verify resilience invariants by injecting faults into non-production environments (and controlled production slices):

  • Sever network links between availability zones using traffic control (tc).
  • Inject artificial latency into database connection drivers.
  • Terminate host instances abruptly during peak throughput tests.
  • Verify that failover mechanics do not trigger secondary failure loops.

11. Architecture Decision Framework

Requirement / Dimension Recommended Recovery Mechanism Primary Trade-Off
Transient Network Jitter Exponential backoff with full jitter + retries Increased request latency
Downstream Outage Circuit breaker + fallback response / shedding Reduced functional capability
Process Deadlock / Hang Liveness probe + automated supervisor restart Brief unavailability during restart
Database Connection Exhaustion Bulkhead pattern + connection pooling limits Rejected client requests (fail-fast)
Split-Brain Network Partition Quorum-based consensus (Raft/Paxos) Write unavailability in minority partition

12. Conclusion

Partial failures are an inevitable characteristic of distributed systems operating at scale. Engineering robust resiliency requires shifting from binary up/down assumptions to continuous failure detection, adaptive isolation, controlled retry mechanics, and rigorous fault injection testing. By enforcing these architectural patterns, systems maintain graceful degradation under pressure and preserve operational integrity across distributed environments.

title: My landing page had no hero. The HTML was correct the whole time.
description:
I found this while taking screenshots for a Product Hunt listing, which is an embarrassing way to discover that the top of your own marketing site has been missing.

The page opened on its second section. The headline, the subheading, the platform badges, the animated terminal and the single call to action button were all absent. Not mispositioned. Absent.

Everything I would normally check said it was fine

This is the part worth writing down, because every instinct I reached for came back green.

curl returned the headline. It is right there in the served HTML:

curl -s https://example.dev | grep -o "Your Next Stack, Sparked"
# Your Next Stack, Sparked

The element existed in the DOM. It had real dimensions:

document.querySelector('h1').getBoundingClientRect()
// { x: 83, y: 336.9, width: 536, height: 48.4 }

No console errors. No failed requests. No hydration warning. A 536x48 heading, sitting at y=337, which is on screen.

So the markup was right, the element was right, the element had a size, and the element was invisible.

The measurement that actually found it

I stopped checking whether things existed and started measuring what the layout was doing. Specifically, the height of every direct child of the scroll container:

const sc = document.querySelector('div.flex-1.min-h-0.overflow-y-auto');
[...sc.children].map(e => ({
  tag: e.tagName,
  offsetTop: e.offsetTop,
  height: Math.round(e.getBoundingClientRect().height),
  text: e.textContent.trim().slice(0, 30),
}));

Which gave me this:

element offsetTop height
hero <section> 57 0
demo video <section> 57 654
features <section> 711 919

Two sections claiming the same offsetTop. The hero was zero pixels tall, so the next section laid out on top of it, and the hero's own overflow-hidden clipped its contents out of existence.

The h1 genuinely was 536x48. It was just 536x48 inside a box with no height, painted underneath the section that came after it.

Why it collapsed

The page shell is one viewport tall and never scrolls itself. A fixed-height flex column holds everything, and one inner div does the scrolling:

<div class="h-dvh overflow-hidden flex flex-col">
  <nav class="shrink-0">...</nav>
  <div class="flex-1 min-h-0 overflow-y-auto flex flex-col">
    <section class="relative overflow-hidden">...</section>  <!-- the hero -->
    <section>...</section>
    <section>...</section>
  </div>
</div>

Every section is a flex item in a fixed-height column, so every section is shrinkable. flex-shrink defaults to 1.

Normally that does not matter, because a flex item's automatic minimum size (min-height: auto) stops it shrinking below its content. That default is what keeps flex columns from crushing themselves.

But min-height: auto only applies when the item's overflow is visible. From the CSS Flexible Box spec: the automatic minimum size is zero when the box is a scroll container, and overflow: hidden makes it one.

The hero was the only section with overflow-hidden on it. So it was the only section whose minimum size was zero. Every other section held its ground, the column still needed to give up space, and the one item that could shrink to nothing did exactly that.

The overflow-hidden was there to clip a decorative background. It was not doing anything I would have thought of as layout.

Proving it before changing anything

Two one line experiments in the console on the live page, before I touched the source:

const hero = document.querySelector('div.flex-1.min-h-0.overflow-y-auto > section:first-child');
const h = () => Math.round(hero.getBoundingClientRect().height);

h();                                 // 0
hero.style.flexShrink = '0'; h();    // 716
hero.style.flexShrink = '';
hero.style.minHeight = 'auto'; h();  // 0

flex-shrink: 0 brings it back. min-height: auto does not, which is the tell: the automatic minimum is already being computed as zero because of the overflow, so restating it changes nothing. That second result is what turns a plausible theory into the actual mechanism.

The fix

One class.

- <section className="relative overflow-hidden">
+ <section className="relative shrink-0 overflow-hidden">

I left a comment on it, because the next person to tidy up a "redundant" utility class will delete it:

shrink-0 is load-bearing. This section is a flex item in the fixed-height
flex column above, so it is shrinkable by default. Every other section keeps
min-height: auto and resists, but overflow-hidden forces this one's automatic
minimum size to zero, so it absorbed the whole overflow and collapsed to 0px.
Do not remove without also removing overflow-hidden.

How to check your own

If you have a fixed-height flex column anywhere, measure the children rather than trusting that the content is present:

[...document.querySelectorAll('section, main > div')]
  .map(e => [e.className.slice(0, 40), Math.round(e.getBoundingClientRect().height)])
  .filter(([, h]) => h === 0);

Anything returning zero while containing real content is this bug. The combination to look for is a flex or grid item that sets overflow to anything other than visible, inside a container with a constrained height.

Worth saying plainly: none of my usual checks could have caught this. Server rendered HTML tests pass, because the HTML is correct. Snapshot tests pass, because the tree is correct. A smoke test asserting the headline is in the document passes. The only thing that catches it is asking the browser how tall the box actually is.

Disclosure

The site is SparkStack, a Next.js starter I sell, so this was my own shop window with the lights off. I do not know exactly how long it was broken, which is its own lesson: I had no check that would have told me. The fix is deployed and the hero has been back at 716 pixels since.

If you take one thing from this, make it the measurement rather than the fix. getBoundingClientRect().height on your layout wrappers costs nothing and tells you something that reading the markup cannot.

title: Container Orchestrators: How Kubernetes Keeps Applications Running When Machines Fail
description:
Container Orchestrators: How Kubernetes Keeps Applications Running When Machines Fail

Container orchestrators maintain application availability during hardware degradation, node drops, and network partitions by continuously evaluating desired system state against actual runtime reality. When an underlying virtual or physical machine crashes, an orchestrator does not wait for manual intervention; it detects the failure via heartbeat timeouts, invalidates the unhealthy node's workload assignments, and reschedules pods onto surviving compute resources. This continuous cycle of observation and correction turns fragile infrastructure into resilient distributed systems, sharing architectural similarities with how systems handle partial failures architecture designing distributed systems for resiliency and recovery and scale under load like database scaling how modern databases stay fast when tables reach billions of rows.

Desired State vs. Actual State

At the core of any modern container orchestrator is a continuous control loop pattern. Rather than executing a one-off imperative script (e.g., "start three containers right now"), operators declare the desired state of the system in configuration files (such as YAML manifests defining a Deployment with three replicas). The orchestrator's control plane continuously queries the actual state of the cluster, comparing telemetry from worker nodes against the target manifest.

+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                    Control Plane                      |
|                                                       |
|   +-------------------+       +-------------------+   |
|   |   API Server      | <---> |    Scheduler      |   |
|   +-------------------+       +-------------------+   |
|             ^                           |             |
|             | (Watches)                 v             |
|   +-------------------+       +-------------------+   |
|   |    Controllers    | <---> |  Desired vs Actual|   |
|   +-------------------+       +-------------------+   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
                                            |
                                            v (Reconciles)
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                      Worker Nodes                     |
|         [Node A: 2 Pods]      [Node B: 1 Pod]         |
+-------------------------------------------------------+

When a discrepancy is detected—such as a worker node going offline, reducing active replicas from three to two—the controller queues a remediation task. Orchestration is fundamentally a continuous control system running feedback loops:

+---------------------------------------------------+
|               Reconciliation Loop                 |
|                                                   |
|   +------------------+     +------------------+   |
|   |  Observe State   | --> |  Compare Target  |   |
|   +------------------+     +------------------+   |
|            ^                        |             |
|            |                        v             |
|   +------------------+     +------------------+   |
|   |   Execute Act    | <-- |  Detect Delta    |   |
|   +------------------+     +------------------+   |
+---------------------------------------------------+

Cluster Architecture & Control Plane Mechanics

An orchestrator's architecture splits cleanly into a control plane (the brain) and worker nodes (the muscle).

The Control Plane

  • API Server (kube-apiserver): The central front-end exposing all REST operations, validating requests, and serving as the data hub for cluster components. It persists all cluster state in a strongly consistent transactional key-value store.
  • Key-Value Store (etcd): A distributed, consistent consensus store implementing the Raft algorithm. It holds the definitive source of truth for cluster configuration, object specs, and status tracking.
  • Scheduler (kube-scheduler): Watches for newly created pods lacking node assignments, evaluates hardware resource requirements, and selects optimal worker nodes based on constraints and affinity rules.
  • Controllers: A collection of background control loops (Node Controller, ReplicaSet Controller, EndpointSlice Controller) that drive the current state toward the declared desired state.

Worker Nodes

  • Kubelet: The primary node agent running on every worker. It registers the node with the API server, monitors assigned pod specs, and drives the container runtime.
  • Container Runtime: The engine responsible for pulling container images, configuring isolation namespaces and cgroups, and executing containers (e.g., containerd, CRI-O).
  • Networking & Storage Plugins (CNI & CSI): Container Network Interfaces assign routable IP addresses or overlay networking to pods, while Container Storage Interfaces attach persistent volumes across node boundaries.

How Work Gets Scheduled

When a workload is admitted into the cluster, the scheduler evaluates placement decisions through a strict two-phase filter and score pipeline.

+-------------------------------------------------------+
|                 Scheduling Pipeline                   |
|                                                       |
|   Unassigned Pod --> [ Filtering Phase ]              |
|                              | (Discard Invalid Nodes)|
|                              v                        |
|                      [ Scoring Phase ]                |
|                              | (Rank Surviving Nodes) |
|                              v                        |
|                      [ Bind to Node ]                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
  1. Filtering (Predicates): The scheduler eliminates nodes incapable of running the workload. It checks if remaining CPU and memory requests exceed node capacity, verifies port bindings, validates node selectors, and evaluates taints and tolerations.
  2. Scoring (Priorities): Surviving nodes are ranked based on resource balancing, image locality (whether the worker node has already cached the container image layer), spreading constraints, and affinity/anti-affinity preferences.
  3. Binding: The scheduler writes the node assignment back to the API server, prompting the target node's Kubelet to initiate container creation.

Container and Application Health

A container process running inside an operating system namespace does not guarantee that the internal web server, database connection pool, or background worker is capable of servicing traffic. Orchestrators utilize multi-layered health probes to verify application viability.

  • Liveness Probes: Determines when to restart a container. If a liveness probe fails repeatedly due to a deadlocked thread or infinite memory leak, the Kubelet kills the container and initiates a restart.
  • Readiness Probes: Determines when a container is ready to accept inbound network traffic. Until a readiness probe returns a success status code, the orchestrator removes the pod's IP address from load balancer endpoints.
  • Startup Probes: Protects slow-starting legacy applications by disabling liveness and readiness checks until initialization completes, preventing premature termination during startup.

Self-Healing and Node Failure Handling

When a hardware failure or kernel panic causes a worker node to drop offline, the control plane initiates automated recovery routines.

Node Loss Detection

Worker nodes maintain liveness through periodic heartbeat signals sent to the API server. If a node stops reporting within a configured timeout window (e.g., node-monitor-grace-period), the Node Controller marks the node's status as NotReady.

Rescheduling and Graceful Eviction

Once a node is declared dead, the ReplicaSet controller notices that the active replica count has fallen below the declared desired state. It schedules replacement pods onto healthy worker nodes. For stateful workloads or persistent volumes attached to crashed nodes, storage control planes must safely detach volumes from the dead host before mounting them on the recovery node to prevent split-brain filesystem corruption.

Rolling Deployments & Zero-Downtime Updates

Deploying application updates requires orchestrators to balance speed with safety. Rolling updates replace old pod instances with new ones incrementally.

  • Max Unavailable: Controls the maximum number of pods that can be offline during the update window.
  • Max Surge: Controls how many extra pods can be created above the desired replica count during the transition.
  • Rollback Capabilities: If new container images fail readiness probes or throw persistent exceptions, the orchestrator halts the rollout and rolls back the deployment revision to the last stable configuration.

Resource Constraints, Saturation, and Noisy Neighbors

Compute resources on worker nodes are finite. Orchestrators manage multi-tenancy and prevent resource starvation via explicit declarations of resource requests and limits.

  • Requests: The guaranteed compute allocation reserved by the scheduler during placement decisions. If a node lacks available request headroom, pods are rejected or scheduled elsewhere.
  • Limits: The hard boundary enforced by kernel cgroups. If a container exceeds its memory limit, the Linux kernel invokes the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer, terminating the offending process instantly.
  • CPU Throttling: When CPU limits are reached, the kernel restricts container execution cycles, increasing request latencies and degrading throughput.

Autoscaling Frameworks

To accommodate fluctuating load without manual intervention, orchestrators employ multi-tier autoscaling systems:

  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): Adjusts the replica count of a deployment based on observed metrics like CPU utilization or custom application telemetry retrieved from metrics servers.
  • Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): Modifies the CPU and memory requests and limits of running containers, occasionally requiring pod restarts to resize cgroup allocations.
  • Cluster Autoscaler: Monitors pending pods that cannot be scheduled due to insufficient cluster-wide node capacity, dynamically provisioning new virtual machines from cloud provider APIs.

Networking and Service Discovery During Failures

When pods crash or migrate across nodes, their IP addresses change. Orchestrators decouple application routing from individual pod lifecycles using abstraction layers.

  • Services & EndpointSlices: Virtual IP abstractions that maintain a dynamic registry of healthy pod IPs matching specific label selectors.
  • Internal DNS: CoreDNS resolves service names to stable cluster IPs, load-balancing requests across available backend endpoints. When instances fail, unhealthy endpoints are dynamically stripped from DNS routing tables.

Stateful Workloads vs. Stateless Workloads

While stateless applications scale horizontally by simply spawning identical replicas, stateful applications (such as databases and distributed key-value stores) require specialized orchestration primitives.

  • Persistent Volume Claims (PVC): Decouples storage lifecycles from pod lifecycles, ensuring data survives container restarts.
  • StatefulSets: Guarantees stable, unique network identifiers, ordered deployment and scaling, and persistent storage bindings mapped 1:1 to individual pod ordinals.

Comprehensive Failure Modes Matrix

The following matrix categorizes common failure modes encountered in production container orchestration environments alongside their root causes and remediation pathways:

Failure Mode Root Architectural Cause Primary Symptom Automated Remediation
Scheduler Overload High API churn, excessive unassigned pods Pending pod queue growth, latency spikes Rate limiting, scheduler sharding, webhook optimization
Control-Plane Outage etcd disk I/O exhaustion, leader election loss API server timeouts, inability to modify state Quorum recovery, storage tier scaling, WAL compaction
Node Failure Hardware crash, kernel panic, hypervisor fault Node NotReady status, dropped heartbeats Pod eviction, rescheduling to healthy worker nodes
Image-Pull Failure Registry rate-limiting, authentication expiration ImagePullBackOff pod phase Image caching, mirror registries, valid image pull secrets
CrashLoopBackOff Application panic, missing environment variable Container exit code non-zero, restart increments Liveness probe tuning, log inspection, config correction
Resource Exhaustion Memory leak, unconstrained allocations OOM killer termination, CPU throttling Adjusting requests/limits, horizontal autoscaling
Storage Failure Detach/attach timeout, cloud API partition Pod stuck in Terminating or ContainerCreating Volume unmounting force-detach, CSI driver restart
Network Partition Overlay CNI breakdown, security group misconfig Inter-pod communication timeout, DNS resolution failure CNI daemonset recovery, routing table verification

Practical Verification: Simulating Failures in Rust

To demonstrate practical orchestration principles, the following Rust command-line utility simulates a lightweight control loop, monitoring worker node health states and automatically triggering container recovery routines when heartbeats expire.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum NodeStatus {
    Healthy,
    NotReady,
    Terminated,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Pod {
    id: String,
    assigned_node: String,
    restart_count: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct ClusterState {
    nodes: HashMap<String, (NodeStatus, Instant)>,
    pods: Vec<Pod>,
}

struct ControlPlane {
    state: Arc<Mutex<ClusterState>>,
}

impl ControlPlane {
    fn new() -> Self {
        let mut nodes = HashMap::new();
        nodes.insert("node-alpha".to_string(), (NodeStatus::Healthy, Instant::now()));
        nodes.insert("node-beta".to_string(), (NodeStatus::Healthy, Instant::now()));

        let pods = vec![
            Pod { id: "web-app-1".to_string(), assigned_node: "node-alpha".to_string(), restart_count: 0 },
            Pod { id: "web-app-2".to_string(), assigned_node: "node-beta".to_string(), restart_count: 0 },
        ];

        Self {
            state: Arc::new(Mutex::new(ClusterState { nodes, pods })),
        }
    }

    fn simulate_node_failure(&self, node_name: &str) {
        let mut cluster = self.state.lock().unwrap();
        if let Some(node) = cluster.nodes.get_mut(node_name) {
            node.0 = NodeStatus::NotReady;
            // Simulate stale timestamp exceeding grace period
            node.1 = Instant::now() - Duration::from_secs(15);
            println!("[SIMULATION] Node '{}' marked as NotReady.", node_name);
        }
    }

    fn run_reconciliation_loop(&self) {
        let state = Arc::clone(&self.state);
        thread::spawn(move || {
            loop {
                thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(2));
                let mut cluster = state.lock().unwrap();
                let now = Instant::now();

                let mut failed_nodes = Vec::new();
                for (name, (status, last_heartbeat)) in cluster.nodes.iter_mut() {
                    if *status == NodeStatus::NotReady && now.duration_since(*last_heartbeat) > Duration::from_secs(10) {
                        *status = NodeStatus::Terminated;
                        failed_nodes.push(name.clone());
                    }
                }

                if !failed_nodes.is_empty() {
                    println!("[RECONCILE] Detected terminated nodes: {:?}", failed_nodes);

                    // Reschedule pods from failed nodes
                    for pod in cluster.pods.iter_mut() {
                        if failed_nodes.contains(&pod.assigned_node) {
                            println!("[SCHEDULER] Evicting pod '{}' from dead node '{}'", pod.id, pod.assigned_node);
                            pod.assigned_node = "node-alpha".to_string(); // Reschedule to healthy node
                            pod.restart_count += 1;
                            println!("[RECONCILE] Pod '{}' successfully rescheduled. Total restarts: {}", pod.id, pod.restart_count);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        });
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("Initializing Container Orchestrator Control Loop...");
    let orchestrator = ControlPlane::new();
    orchestrator.run_reconciliation_loop();

    // Let the system run healthy for 1 second
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));

    // Simulate catastrophic node failure
    orchestrator.simulate_node_failure("node-beta");

    // Allow reconciliation loop to process failure
    thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(4));
    println!("Orchestration verification complete.");
}

Verification Commands

To compile and execute the simulation harness:

cargo init --bin orchestrator_sim
cd orchestrator_sim
# Paste code into src/main.rs
cargo run --release

Architecture Decision Framework

When designing distributed architectures, evaluating whether to adopt container orchestration requires weighing operational overhead against workload complexity:

+-------------------------------------------------------+
|             Orchestration Decision Tree               |
|                                                       |
|   Are there multi-tenant microservices?               |
|     ├── YES -> Adopt Container Orchestrator (K8s)     |
|     └── NO  -> Evaluate PaaS / Serverless / Compose   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
  • Workload Scale: Monolithic single-instance deployments gain minimal benefit from complex orchestrators and incur unnecessary control-plane management overhead. Conversely, distributed microservice architectures with dozens of dependent services require automated orchestration.
  • Stateful vs. Stateless Services: Stateless web services are trivial to orchestrate and recover. Stateful workloads require rigorous provisioning of persistent storage primitives, backup pipelines, and careful split-brain mitigation strategies.
  • Operational Expertise: Operating a highly available control plane (managing etcd consensus, certificate rotation, and CNI upgrades) demands dedicated platform engineering competencies. If cluster maintenance overhead outweighs development velocity, managed control planes or simpler container platforms should be prioritized.

Originally published at WantsVibes.

Explore in-depth systems architecture breakdowns, distributed systems guides, and AI engineering benchmarks on WantsVibes.online.

title: Building PWAs: The Offline-First Quest (A Hobbit's Journey)
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Ever clicked a link on your phone only to stare at the dreaded “No Internet” dinosaur while you’re stuck on a spotty train? I’ve been there, more times than I care to admit. I was building a simple weather dashboard for a side project, and every time the user lost connectivity the whole thing just… died. It felt like sending a raven into a storm and watching it get swallowed whole.

That frustration lit a fire: I wanted my web app to behave more like a native app—still useful when the network decides to take a coffee break. Enter Progressive Web Apps, the offline‑first superpower that lets you keep the adventure going even when the Wi‑Fi gremlins strike.

The Revelation (The Insight)

The magic trick behind PWAs isn’t some alien tech; it’s a humble service worker—a script that runs in the background, intercepting network requests and serving cached responses when the network is unavailable. Think of it as your own personal Gandalf, whispering “You shall not pass… to the error page” and instead handing you a cached copy of the UI.

When I first wrapped my head around the caching strategies—Cache‑First, Network‑First, Stale‑While‑Revalidate—it felt like discovering a secret map in an old textbook. Suddenly, I could decide what to keep offline (the shell, the core assets) and what to fetch fresh (the latest data). The realization that I could make a web app feel instant and reliable without asking users to install anything from an app store was pure wizardry.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

1. Registering the Service Worker

First things first: we need to tell the browser about our trusty sidekick.

// src/registerSW.js
if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  window.addEventListener('load', () => {
    navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')
      .then(reg => console.log('Service Worker registered ✅', reg.scope))
      .catch(err => console.error('Service Worker registration failed ❌', err));
  });
}

Common trap: Forgetting to call this script from your main HTML (or calling it too early). If the registration never runs, you’ll never see the offline magic. Place the script at the bottom of <body> or defer it with type="module".

2. The Service Worker Itself (sw.js)

Here’s where we define our caching strategy. I’ll show a Cache‑First approach for static assets and a Network‑First fallback for API data—mirroring how a hobbit packs lembas bread for the journey but still checks for fresh water at the stream.

// sw.js
const CACHE_NAME = 'weather-pwa-v1';
const STATIC_ASSETS = [
  '/',
  '/index.html',
  '/styles.css',
  '/app.js',
  '/icons/icon-192.png',
  '/icons/icon-512.png'
];

// Install – cache the static shell
self.addEventListener('install', event => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE_NAME)
      .then(cache => cache.addAll(STATIC_ASSETS))
      .then(() => self.skipWaiting())
  );
});

// Activate – clean up old caches
self.addEventListener('activate', event => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.keys()
      .then(keys => Promise.all(
        keys.filter(key => key !== CACHE_NAME)
              .map(key => caches.delete(key))
      ))
      .then(() => self.clients.claim())
  );
});

// Fetch – our core logic
self.addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  const { request } = event;

  // Skip cross‑origin requests (like third‑party analytics)
  if (!request.url.startsWith(self.location.origin)) return;

  // API calls – Network first, fallback to cache
  if (request.url.includes('/api/weather')) {
    event.respondWith(
      fetch(request)
        .then(response => {
          // Optional: clone and put a fresh copy in the cache
          return caches.open(CACHE_NAME).then(cache => {
            cache.put(request, response.clone());
            return response;
          });
        })
        .catch(() => caches.match(request)) // if network fails, serve cached
    );
    return;
  }

  // Everything else – Cache first, then network
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(request)
      .then(cachedResp => cachedResp || fetch(request))
  );
});

Common trap: Caching the API response indiscriminately. If you cache a POST or a request with varying query strings without proper keys, you’ll serve stale data to everyone. In the snippet above we only cache GET requests to /api/weather and we clone the response before storing it—otherwise the stream would be consumed and the fetch would fail.

3. Making the App Installable

A manifest.json gives the browser the metadata it needs to offer the “Add to Home screen” prompt.

// manifest.json
{
  "name": "WeatherWizard PWA",
  "short_name": "WeatherWizard",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#ffffff",
  "theme_color": "#0d6efd",
  "icons": [
    {
      "src": "/icons/icon-192.png",
      "sizes": "192x192",
      "type": "image/png"
    },
    {
      "src": "/icons/icon-512.png",
      "sizes": "512x512",
      "type": "image/png"
    }
  ]
}

Link it in your HTML:

<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">

When the user visits on a supported browser, they’ll see a subtle banner inviting them to install the app—no app store required.

4. Offline Fallback Page (The “You’re Offline” Message)

Sometimes you want a friendly note instead of a blank screen. Add this to your fetch handler:

// inside the fetch event, after trying cache/network
.catch(() => caches.match('/offline.html'));

And create a simple offline.html that uses only cached assets (maybe a cute illustration and a retry button).

Why This New Power Matters

With these few dozen lines, your web app transforms from a fragile house of cards into a sturdy cottage that can weather a network storm. Users get instant loading on repeat visits, data stays available during commutes or flights, and you earn that sweet, sweet “installable” badge without wrestling with native SDKs.

I still remember the first time I turned off my Wi‑Fi, refreshed the page, and saw my weather dashboard still displaying the last forecast—complete with icons and layout. It felt like Neo dodging bullets in The Matrix when the fallback kicked in: smooth, unexpected, and utterly satisfying.

Now you can ship features that work everywhere—from a bustling coffee shop to a mountaintop with zero bars. That’s the real superpower of PWAs: the web becomes resilient, and your users stay engaged no matter what.

Your Turn, Adventurer

Ready to embark on your own offline‑first quest? Take an existing project (maybe that blog you’ve been tinkering with) and add a service worker using the patterns above. Start with caching the static shell, then experiment with a network‑first strategy for your API.

When you see your app survive a deliberate navigator.connection.downlink = 0 test (or just flip airplane mode), come back and share your story. What did you cache first? What surprising thing did you learn about your users’ offline habits?

The road is open, the map is in your hands—go build something that works even when the internet decides to take a nap. Happy coding! 🚀

title: Context API vs Redux
description:
The question is usually framed as "which one is better", but that's the wrong question. Context and Redux do different jobs. The important part is understanding how each one updates its consumers.

👉 Try it in practice: Shopping Cart with Context

What Context actually does

Context lets a component read and subscribe to a value without threading it down through props. The context object itself does not hold data; it only describes what can be provided and read. To make the value change, you pair the provider with useState or useReducer.

const ThemeContext = createContext("light");

function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState("light");
  return (
    <ThemeContext value={theme}>
      <Page />
    </ThemeContext>
  );
}

The key detail, from the React docs: when the value you pass to a provider changes, React re-renders every component that reads that context. It compares the old and new values with Object.is. There are no selectors, so you can't subscribe to just one field of the value.

What Redux adds

Redux is a centralized store with a single flow: action, reducer, store. Around that flow you get middleware, Redux DevTools, and an action history, so you can answer "when did this slice change and where did the data come from?".

Its real advantage over Context is useSelector. A component subscribes to the result it selects, not to the whole store:

const count = useSelector((s) => s.cart.items.length);
const theme = useSelector((s) => s.theme.mode);

Change cart and the component reading theme does not re-render. With Context, it would.

The re-render difference

A Context subscription is to the context value as a whole, not to individual fields. Put { user, cart, theme } in a single context and changing cart re-renders the component that only reads theme too. You can fix this by splitting into multiple contexts and memoizing values, but that's work you do by hand. Redux gives you granular subscriptions through selectors.

When to use each

Context for simple shared values with few consumers: theme, locale, current user, and state scoped to one feature. Zero dependencies.

Redux when shared client state gets large, is used in many places, or has update logic that's getting complex. It also helps when you need to inspect how state changes over time with Redux DevTools.

Data fetched from an API is server state and belongs in SWR or React Query, not in either of these.

A real example: the shopping cart

A cart with a few items, a header badge, and a checkout button is fine in Context.

Watch what happens as it grows: a coupon field, a quantity stepper, a "save for later" list. Now items, coupon, and saved share one context. Updating items re-renders the coupon and saved consumers too. Put the coupon draft in that same context and every keystroke re-renders the header badge.

That's where selectors earn their keep: components can subscribe to different slices of state independently, and a component re-renders only when the piece it reads changes. Redux DevTools and action history are the bonus on top.

Start with Context. Reach for a store when the state and its consumers get complex enough to justify it, not before.

👉 Build both and compare: Shopping Cart with Redux

title: LEO Satellite Networks: Routing Internet Traffic Across Moving Constellations
description:
LEO Satellite Networks: Routing Internet Traffic Across Moving Constellations

Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations introduce a fundamentally non-traditional networking challenge: the physical topology of the network is in continuous, highly predictable motion relative to the ground stations and user terminals it serves. Traditional terrestrial and data center networking assumes a static physical topology where link weights and adjacency states change only during failures, maintenance windows, or active traffic engineering. In contrast, LEO networks operate at orbital velocities ranging from 7 to 8 kilometers per second, requiring dynamic routing algorithms, predictive link-state calculations, and rigorous handover mechanisms to maintain session continuity.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        LEO Network End-to-End Data Path                         |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

  [ User Terminal ] 
         |
         v (RF Uplink)
  [ LEO Satellite A ] <---(Optical/RF ISL)---> [ LEO Satellite B ]
         |                                              |
         v (RF Downlink)                                v (RF Downlink)
  [ Ground Gateway A ]                           [ Ground Gateway B ]
         |                                              |
         +-------------------[ Terrestrial Core ]-------+
                                        |
                                        v
                             [ Internet Destination ]

1. Context & Problem Statement

Terrestrial IP routing relies on the stability of physical fiber paths. Routers exchange state via Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) like OSPF or IS-IS, or Exterior Gateway Protocols like BGP, assuming that a connected interface or neighbor adjacency remains physically stationary. LEO satellite constellations invalidate this assumption across multiple dimensions:

  • Continuous Relocation: Satellites transit the sky in minutes, causing the set of visible neighbor satellites and ground stations to change second by second.
  • Dynamic Propagation Delays: As a satellite approaches and recedes from a user terminal or ground gateway, the geometric distance—and therefore the propagation delay—fluctuates dynamically.
  • Intermittent Visibility: Ground-to-satellite paths are subject to horizon masking, atmospheric attenuation, and line-of-sight obstructions, requiring rapid path recalculation.
  • Asymmetric Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs): Satellites communicate via free-space optical (FSO) or radio frequency (RF) inter-satellite links. These links must establish and maintain precise pointing, acquisition, and tracking (PAT) alignments under thermal expansion and orbital drift.

Engineering a resilient LEO data plane requires combining predictable orbital mechanics with real-time control-plane telemetry, balancing routing table churn against convergence speed.

2. Architectural Decision Record (ADR)

ADR-01: Proactive Orbital-Predictive Routing vs. Reactive Link-State Flooding

  • Context: LEO satellites must continuously update routing tables as neighbor adjacencies break and form due to orbital motion. Traditional reactive link-state routing protocols (e.g., OSPF flooding every topology change) generate excessive control-plane overhead over constrained space-to-space links and struggle to maintain stability under high churn.
  • Decision: Implement a hybrid proactive-reactive routing architecture where baseline topology updates are computed deterministically ahead of time using known ephemeris data (orbital parameters), while unexpected link failures or atmospheric degradation trigger reactive localized path adjustments.
  • Consequences:
    • Positive: Drastically reduces control-plane messaging overhead across ISLs, allowing more bandwidth for the data plane. Predictable schedule changes are pre-loaded into routing engines.
    • Negative: Requires tightly synchronized clocks across the constellation and complex onboard ephemeris calculation engines to predict adjacency lifetimes accurately.
    • Alternatives Considered: Pure reactive OSPF/IS-IS flooding (rejected due to excessive control-plane congestion) and purely centralized terrestrial routing control (rejected due to high propagation latency to ground controllers).

ADR-02: Inter-Satellite Link (ISL) Medium Selection: Optical vs. Radio Frequency

  • Context: Satellites require high-bandwidth backbone links to route traffic across oceans and remote regions where ground gateways are absent.
  • Decision: Utilize free-space optical (FSO) laser links for primary inter-satellite trunking, supplemented by Ka/Ku-band RF links for backup and low-elevation scenarios.
  • Consequences:
    • Positive: Optical links provide multi-gigabit to terabit-per-second capacities with high immunity to RF interference and interception.
    • Negative: Strict pointing, acquisition, and tracking (PAT) requirements under orbital vibration; susceptibility to cloud attenuation when links drop close to the atmosphere.
    • Alternatives Considered: Pure RF ISLs (rejected due to spectrum licensing constraints and lower aggregate bandwidth density).

3. System Topology & Component Model

The end-to-end LEO networking architecture comprises five distinct physical and logical domains:

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        LEO System Component Interaction                         |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

  +------------------+         +------------------+         +------------------+
  |  User Terminal   | <-----> |  LEO Satellite   | <-----> | Inter-Satellite  |
  |    (UT / CPE)    |         | (Payload/Router) |         | Link (Optical)   |
  +------------------+         +------------------+         +------------------+
                                        |                             |
                                        v                             v
                               +------------------+         +------------------+
                               |  Ground Gateway  |         | Network Control  |
                               | (Teleport/PoP)   |         | System (NCS)     |
                               +------------------+         +------------------+
                                        |
                                        v
                               +------------------+
                               | Terrestrial Core |
                               |    & Internet    |
                               +------------------+

Core Components

  • User Terminals (UT): Customer premises equipment (phased-array antennas) tracking visible satellites via electronic beam steering.
  • Satellites: Spaceborne nodes containing transponders or full IP-routing payloads, interconnected via optical ISLs forming a space-based mesh network.
  • Ground Stations / Gateways: Terrestrial teleports linking the space segment to regional internet exchange points (IXPs) and core fiber backbones.
  • Network Control Systems (NCS): Ground-based or distributed spaceborne orchestration engines that monitor constellation health, manage ephemeris databases, and compute global routing matrices.

4. Component Interface Signatures

To ensure interoperability between spaceborne routers, ground stations, and orchestration controllers, communication interfaces are defined using structured schema contracts.

Interface Definition: Satellite Ephemeris & Adjacency State (Protobuf Schema) 

syntax = "proto3";

package leo.routing.v1;

message EphemerisRecord {
  uint32 satellite_id = 1;
  double timestamp_epoch_seconds = 2;
  double position_x_meters = 3;
  double position_y_meters = 4;
  double position_z_meters = 5;
  double velocity_vx = 6;
  double velocity_vy = 7;
  double velocity_vz = 8;
}

message AdjacencyState {
  uint32 source_satellite_id = 1;
  uint32 target_satellite_id = 2;
  enum LinkType {
    LINK_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED = 0;
    LINK_TYPE_OPTICAL_FSO = 1;
    LINK_TYPE_RF_RADIO = 2;
  }
  LinkType link_type = 3;
  float available_bandwidth_mbps = 4;
  float current_propagation_delay_ms = 5;
  bool is_active = 6;
}

message TopologyUpdateEvent {
  uint32 sequence_number = 1;
  repeated EphemerisRecord ephemerides = 2;
  repeated AdjacencyState adjacencies = 3;
}

Interface Definition: Gateway Routing Policy (JSON Schema) 

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "GatewayRoutingPolicy",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "gateway_id": { "type": "string" },
    "max_acceptable_latency_ms": { "type": "number" },
    "preferred_uplink_frequency_band": { 
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["Ku", "Ka", "Q/V"]
    },
    "congestion_threshold_percent": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 50, "maximum": 95 },
    "failover_gateway_ids": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": { "type": "string" }
    }
  },
  "required": ["gateway_id", "max_acceptable_latency_ms", "congestion_threshold_percent"]
}

5. Distributed Failure Modes & Mitigations

Operating networking hardware in orbital environments introduces failure modes unique to vacuum, thermal cycling, and radiation:

Failure Mode Root Cause Impact Mitigation Strategy
ISL Pointing Loss Orbital drift, thermal flexing, vibrational jitter Abrupt severance of inter-satellite trunk link Automated re-acquisition sweeping, multi-beam optical redundancy, rapid fallback to RF backup links.
Gateway Bottlenecking High concentration of regional traffic converging on a single teleport Queue buildup, packet drop, high jitter Anycast gateway routing, dynamic traffic load-shaping, and proactive redirection via ISLs to uncongested regional gateways.
Handover Drop UT beam steering lag during satellite horizon transition Session reset, packet loss during handoff Make-before-break dual-connectivity handovers, multi-path tunneling across overlapping satellite footprints.
Radiation Upset (SEU) Cosmic rays inducing bit flips in router memory or FPGA configuration Node crash or routing table corruption Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR), error-correcting code (ECC) memory, watchdog timer reboots.

6. Consequence & Trade-Off Matrix

Architectural Dimension Proactive Orbital Routing Reactive Link-State Flooding Hybrid Predictive Routing
Control-Plane Overhead Minimal (Computed offline) Very High (Continuous flooding) Low-to-Moderate (Ephemeris-driven + localized alerts)
Convergence Latency Instantaneous (Pre-calculated) High (Depends on propagation and timer delays) Low (Fast path reroute on failure event)
Hardware Complexity High (Requires onboard ephemeris engines) Low (Standard routing daemons) High (Requires synchronization between predictive and reactive modules)
Resilience to Anomalies Poor against unpredicted failures High (Adapts to any arbitrary failure) High (Pre-computed paths + dynamic failure bypass)

7. Operational Realism: Latency\, Handovers\, and Traffic Engineering

Why LEO Does Not Mean "Zero-Latency"

While LEO orbits (500 km to 1,200 km) reduce propagation delays compared to Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) satellites (~35,786 km), physical laws still govern latency:

  • Free-Space Propagation: Light travels at approximately $3 $\times$ 10^8$ m/s in a vacuum. A 600 km slant range introduces an irreducible ~4 ms one-way propagation delay per hop.
  • Queueing and Serialization: Multi-hop ISL paths accumulate serialization and queueing delays at each onboard router node.
  • Gateway Backhaul: Traffic delivered via satellite must eventually egress to terrestrial fiber networks, adding terrestrial tail latency.

Satellite Handovers and Session Continuity

Because a LEO satellite remains visible to a given ground terminal for only 5 to 15 minutes, handovers are frequent.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       Make-Before-Break Handover Flow                           |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

  User Terminal         Satellite A (Current)        Satellite B (Target)
       |                         |                             |
       |--- 1. Measure RSSI ---->|                             |
       |--- 2. Detect Horizon -->|                             |
       |                         |--- 3. Coordinate Handover ->|
       |--- 4. Establish Link -------------------------------->|
       |--- 5. Switch Active Path ---------------------------->|
       |                         |--- 6. Tear Down Old Link -->|
  1. Measurement: The user terminal continuously measures Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) and Doppler shift from visible satellites.
  2. Target Selection: Based on orbital trajectory and elevation angle, the terminal selects the incoming satellite.
  3. Make-Before-Break: The terminal establishes a synchronized radio link with the target satellite before severing the connection with the departing satellite, preventing dropped TCP connections and session resets.

8. Conclusion

Routing traffic across a LEO satellite constellation requires an architectural paradigm shift away from static terrestrial assumptions. By synthesizing predictable orbital mechanics with hybrid proactive-reactive routing protocols, resilient inter-satellite optical links, and make-before-break handovers, modern space-based networks achieve enterprise-grade reliability and performance across highly dynamic physical topologies.
